I think there's a good chance that a strong component of why AI-assisted software engineering is the most effective application of LLMs is because software engineers have already deeply internalized the "inputs -> outputs" mentality, and instinctively don't think there's a "someone else" that's responsible for changing the behavior of the system. It's always the inputs that determine the outputs.

If you find yourself complaining about interactions with LLMs starting with the words "The AI XYZ ...," consider instead starting with the words "The way I'm prompting this, I'm noticing XYZ..." This helps mindset shift helps us see better see how to achieve our aims with LLMs.

There's a comparison here to relationships with other humans. If you say to another human, "you make me feel angry," that divests you of agency. If you say to another human, "when you do/say XYZ, then I often find that afterward I am feeling ABC," it opens up the discussion from a point of curiosity.

I love the idea of AI/Coding/Dark Factory: software engineers move up a level from typing code to designing specifications, scenario suites, and validation harnesses that coding agents execute repeatedly. The point is not "no quality bar" - it is replacing manual code review with stronger system-level evidence (holdout scenarios, probabilistic satisfaction metrics, and massive automated scenario throughput).

Another awesome post from Simon at https://github.com/simonw/research illustrating how fast the world is moving, plus two new CLIs he put out: showboat for agents to demo AI coding work and rodney for agents to connect to Chrome DevTools.

Observation on MCP auth reliability: in my experience, MCP is flakier for authentication across specific clients than using direct command-line tools with API keys. With Atlassian MCP, Cursor CLI and Cursor Desktop both seem buggy around auth state; authenticating one can break the other, and if Cursor Desktop is open it can even break Atlassian MCP auth in Cursor CLI. I've also seen OAuth handshake/session-sharing issues across other AI coding agents, where sessions are not reliably shared. MCP is often described as a solution to auth fragmentation, but in practice I keep hitting auth instability, while API keys work reliably every time across my agents.

At the same time that I agree with Person/Dan Shapiro in this blog post, it's tough for me to know how to put aside Person/Steve Yegge's recent comments, who literally wrote a book titled Vibe Coding, and said here https://youtu.be/s96O9oWI_tI?si=Zrp6Hlx6wCywL_IW something I've felt in this last year: it's just as hard as regular coding; you're wrestling with it all day long and it uses gaslighting and deception to fool you into thinking it's at 100% when it's actually only at 60-80%, at least unless and until you put in layers and layers of custom verification, alignment, and cleanup processes.
